How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization

Alexander Gaponov  Grigory Malinovsky  Egor Shulgin  Peter Richtárik ††thanks: Contacts: agaponov04@gmail.com Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
KAUST Center of Excellence for Generative AI
Thuwal, Saudi Arabia
Abstract

Training deep neural networks requires optimizers that balance computational efficiency with formal data privacy. While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. By analyzing Muon’s orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error. This yields an 𝒪(K−1/4)\mathcal{O}(K^{-1/4}) convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) budget, the standard (d/(n​ε))1/2(\sqrt{d}/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2} privacy–utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy. Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size.

1 Introduction

Adaptive methods such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) and AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) remain the default choice for training large models (Achiam et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). A prominent recent alternative is Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), which applies an approximate orthogonalization to the momentum of matrix-valued parameters. Muon has attracted considerable attention due to its strong empirical performance, efficient GPU implementation, and reduced optimizer-state memory; its scalability has been demonstrated by training the Moonlight 16B Mixture-of-Experts model on 5.7 trillion tokens (Liu et al., 2025). Its update can be interpreted through stochastic spectral descent (Carlson et al., 2015; Kovalev et al., 2018) and, more generally, as a step along a linear minimization oracle (LMO) over a norm ball (Jaggi, 2013; Pethick et al., 2025). The LMO view gives a unified treatment of non-Euclidean methods with momentum, recovering normalized SGD (Levy, 2016; Cutkosky and Mehta, 2020), SignSGD and Signum (Bernstein et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2023), Scion (Pethick et al., 2025), and Muon as special cases.

In this work, we study whether, and how, the advantages of momentum orthogonalization carry over to differential privacy (DP). We consider the standard central, example-level setting of DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016): each per-example gradient is clipped to norm cc, Gaussian noise is added to the average, and the result is passed to the optimizer; the momentum and LMO steps are post-processing and do not affect privacy (Dwork et al., 2014). The optimization problem, however, becomes substantially more delicate. Active clipping introduces a state-dependent bias, privacy noise is injected at every step, momentum aggregates gradients along a changing trajectory, and the noisy momentum is then passed through a nonlinear map. Existing analyses of private nonconvex optimization typically sidestep active clipping: the sharpest rates assume Lipschitz losses, that is, uniformly bounded per-example gradients, so that clipping at a threshold above the bound is inactive (Bassily et al., 2021; Tran and Cutkosky, 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Arora et al., 2023; Lowy et al., 2024), and analyses of private distributed methods make similar assumptions (Appendix F). Generic analyses of biased stochastic gradients (Ajalloeian and Stich, 2020; Demidovich et al., 2023) measure the full additive bias and do not exploit the structure of the update.

Key observation: for an LMO, clipping is (almost) a rescaling.

Let μ⁡(g):=𝔼⁡[clipc​(g+ξ)]\mu(g):=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi)] be the expected clipped gradient, where gg is the true gradient and ξ\xi is zero-mean sampling noise with variance σ2\sigma^{2}. We show (Lemma 1) that

μ(g)=λ(g)g+r(g),λ(g)≍cmax⁡{c,‖g‖2},‖r⁡(g)‖2≲λ⁡(g)​min⁡{σ,σ2c}.\begin{gathered}\mu(g)=\lambda(g)\,g+r(g),\qquad\lambda(g)\asymp\frac{c}{\max\{c,\|g\|_{2}\}},\\ \|r(g)\|_{2}\lesssim\lambda(g)\min\Bigl\{\sigma,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c}\Bigr\}.\end{gathered} (1)

The leading effect of clipping is thus a positive rescaling of the true gradient, and an LMO is blind to it: LMO⁡(λ​g)=LMO⁡(g)\mathrm{LMO}(\lambda g)=\mathrm{LMO}(g) for every λ>0\lambda>0. Only the residual r⁡(g)r(g), which changes the direction, enters the optimization error. This lets us analyze momentum-LMO methods under active clipping assuming only bounded centered variance, without bounded gradients and without a clipping threshold that grows with the horizon.

Contributions.

Our answer to the question in the title has a theoretical and an empirical part.

  • •

    Clipping as rescaling. We prove the positive-ray decomposition (1) and a matching bound on the variance of clipped gradients relative to λ⁡(g)\lambda(g) (Section 3).

  • •

    Convergence of private momentum-LMO methods. For smooth nonconvex objectives in any finite-dimensional norm (covering Muon, Scion, sign descent, and normalized SGD), we prove a high-probability bound that separates optimization error, momentum tracking, sampling noise, privacy noise, and a clipping floor ρ1​min⁡{σ,σ2/c}\rho_{1}\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\} (Theorem 1). The floor is the dual-norm version of the tight Euclidean floor of clipped SGD (Koloskova et al., 2023) and vanishes as σ→0\sigma\to 0; passing through the LMO thus costs at most the norm-conversion constant ρ1\rho_{1} relative to clipped SGD, and the guarantee does not show that it improves on it. At a fixed noise scale, the bound gives the rate 𝒪~(K−1/4)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{-1/4}), where 𝒪~\widetilde{\mathcal{O}} hides factors logarithmic in KK and in the failure probability; and with noise calibrated to an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) budget it gives the familiar 𝒪⁡((c​𝔼​‖Z‖⋆​log⁡(1/δ)/(n​ε))1/2)\mathcal{O}\big((c\,\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2}\big) dependence (Corollary 1, Appendix C.2).

  • •

    What changes under DP. On CNN and a 30M-parameter GPT model, we sweep the batch size, learning rate, and momentum for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon (and Scion). Under DP, the optimal batch size grows by one to two orders of magnitude and the ranking of optimizers depends on the batch size, unlike in non-private training, where Muon is best at every batch size. On CIFAR-10, DP-Muon attains the lowest mean test loss at all but one batch size, with the gaps within one standard deviation at intermediate batch sizes; on language modeling, DP-Muon is best at small batch sizes, DP-Adam near the optimal batch size, and Scion at large batch sizes (Section 4).

Concurrent work.

Two concurrent and independent works also study private Muon11 1 Both also use the name “DP-Muon” for closely related algorithms.. Kim and Fan (2026) analyze a Muon variant with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) orthogonalization and propose a bias-corrected DP-MuonBC; their vanishing-rate corollaries assume moment bounds on the raw (uncentered) per-example gradients and let the clipping threshold grow with the horizon, while their general bound contains a clipping term that persists even without sampling noise. Shanmugam et al. (2026) study when orthogonalization recovers useful singular directions of privatized gradients through a Wedin-type signal-to-noise argument and report large gains of DP-Muon over DP-SGD in vision at large batch sizes. Our analysis is complementary: it covers general LMO geometries, requires only centered variance, and isolates the part of the clipping bias that an LMO actually sees; a detailed comparison is given in Section 3.3 and Appendix E.

2 Setup and Algorithm

We consider minx∈𝒳⁡f⁡(x):=1n​∑i=1nfi​(x)\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}f(x):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(x) over a finite-dimensional normed space (𝒳,∥⋅∥)(\mathcal{X},\|\cdot\|) with dual norm ‖v‖⋆:=sup‖d‖≤1⟨v,d⟩\|v\|_{\star}:=\sup_{\|d\|\leq 1}\langle v,d\rangle. For the unit ball 𝒞={v:‖v‖≤1}\mathcal{C}=\{v:\|v\|\leq 1\}, the linear minimization oracle is LMO⁡(g)∈arg⁡minv∈𝒞​⟨g,v⟩\mathrm{LMO}(g)\in\arg\min_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\langle g,v\rangle, so that ⟨g,LMO⁡(g)⟩=−‖g‖⋆\langle g,\mathrm{LMO}(g)\rangle=-\|g\|_{\star} and LMO⁡(λ​g)=LMO⁡(g)\mathrm{LMO}(\lambda g)=\mathrm{LMO}(g) for λ>0\lambda>0. The spectral norm on a weight matrix gives Muon, LMO⁡(G)=−U​V⊤\mathrm{LMO}(G)=-UV^{\top} for G=U​Σ​V⊤G=U\Sigma V^{\top}; the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm gives sign descent; the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm gives normalized gradient descent; and layer-wise combinations give Scion (Pethick et al., 2025) (see Table 2 in the appendix). Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite-dimensional, there are constants ρ1,ρ2\rho_{1},\rho_{2} with ‖v‖⋆≤ρ1​‖v‖2\|v\|_{\star}\leq\rho_{1}\|v\|_{2} and ‖v‖2≤ρ2​‖v‖⋆\|v\|_{2}\leq\rho_{2}\|v\|_{\star}; for the spectral norm on an m×n′m\times n^{\prime} matrix, ∥⋅∥⋆\|\cdot\|_{\star} is the nuclear norm, ρ1=min⁡{m,n′}\rho_{1}=\sqrt{\min\{m,n^{\prime}\}}, and ρ2=1\rho_{2}=1. Clipping is Euclidean, clipc​(v):=v​min⁡{1,c/‖v‖2}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(v):=v\min\{1,c/\|v\|_{2}\}, as in DP-SGD.

DP-Muon (Algorithm 1) privatizes the mini-batch gradient exactly as DP-SGD does; only the optimizer step differs. In practice, Muon is applied with a few Newton–Schulz iterations in place of the exact polar factor; our analysis assumes an exact LMO.

A randomized algorithm ℳ\mathcal{M} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private if ℙ⁡(ℳ⁡(𝒟)∈S)≤eε​ℙ​(ℳ⁡(𝒟′)∈S)+δ\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})\in S)\leq e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\in S)+\delta for all measurable SS and all adjacent datasets 𝒟,𝒟′\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime} (Dwork et al., 2014). We use add/remove adjacency (one example added or removed) for Poisson subsampling, as in Abadi et al. (2016), and replace-one adjacency for fixed-size sampling without replacement (Wang et al., 2019); an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP guarantee under add/remove adjacency implies (2​ε,(1+eε)​δ)(2\varepsilon,(1+e^{\varepsilon})\delta)-DP under replace-one adjacency, but not conversely.

Proposition 1 (Privacy).

Let x0x_{0}, KK, BB, cc, σDP\sigma_{\rm DP}, α\alpha, and γ\gamma be fixed independently of the data (and, under replace-one adjacency, nn be public), and let the output be the whole trajectory x0,…,xKx_{0},\dots,x_{K}, so that any function of it, such as the tail average or a uniformly sampled iterate, inherits the guarantee. Proof sketch.

The first claim is the post-processing property of differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2014), applied with adaptive composition over the KK releases g^k\hat{g}_{k}. For fixed-size sampling, replacing one example changes the clipped sum ∑i∈Skclipc​(∇fi​(xk))\sum_{i\in S_{k}}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(\nabla f_{i}(x_{k})) by at most 2​c2c in ℓ2\ell_{2}, so each release is a Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier σmult=B​σDP\sigma_{\rm mult}=B\sigma_{\rm DP} relative to sensitivity cc. For the subsampled Gaussian mechanism, Wang et al. (2019, Theorem 9 and the discussion after it) give the Rényi-DP bound ε′​(a)=𝒪⁡(q2​a/σmult2)\varepsilon^{\prime}(a)=\mathcal{O}(q^{2}a/\sigma_{\rm mult}^{2}) at small orders aa and large σmult\sigma_{\rm mult}; the replace-one sensitivity 2​c2c only changes the constant. Composing over KK steps and converting to (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) with an order a≍log⁡(1/δ)/εa\asymp\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon, exactly as in the proof of Abadi et al. (2016, Theorem 1), gives (2); the requirement that this order lies in the range where the bound holds is what imposes ε<c1​q2​K\varepsilon<c_{1}q^{2}K. ∎

Note that, for a fixed number of steps KK, the noise scale on the averaged gradient, c​σDPc\,\sigma_{\rm DP}, does not depend on BB; at a fixed budget of epochs, K∝1/BK\propto 1/B and the noise on the average decreases with BB only through the smaller number of steps (Appendix D.1 quantifies this with the accountant actually used in the experiments).

3 Theory: How Muon Handles Clipping

3.1 Clipping is a rescaling up to a small residual

For a fixed point xx, write g=∇f​(x)g=\nabla f(x) and ξi=∇fi​(x)−g\xi_{i}=\nabla f_{i}(x)-g, so that μ⁡(g)=1n​∑iclipc​(g+ξi)\mu(g)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi_{i}) is the expected clipped mini-batch gradient, and let ac​(g):=c/max⁡{c,‖g‖2}a_{c}(g):=c/\max\{c,\|g\|_{2}\} denote the factor by which gg itself would be clipped.

Lemma 1 (Positive-ray decomposition).

Under Assumption 2, for every gg there is λ⁡(g)∈[14​ac​(g), 2​ac​(g)]\lambda(g)\in[\tfrac{1}{4}a_{c}(g),\,2a_{c}(g)] such that

‖μ⁡(g)−λ⁡(g)​g‖2≤16​λ​(g)​min⁡{σ,σ2c},\|\mu(g)-\lambda(g)g\|_{2}\leq 16\,\lambda(g)\min\Bigl\{\sigma,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c}\Bigr\},

and 1n​∑i‖clipc​(g+ξi)−μ⁡(g)‖22≤320​λ​(g)2​σ2\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\|\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi_{i})-\mu(g)\|_{2}^{2}\leq 320\,\lambda(g)^{2}\sigma^{2}.

The scale λ⁡(g)\lambda(g) is comparable to the clipping factor of the true gradient, so the residual is small relative to the shrunken signal λ⁡(g)​g\lambda(g)g: the clipped mean points in the right direction up to an angle controlled by min⁡{σ,σ2/c}/‖g‖2\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\}/\|g\|_{2}. When c≥σc\geq\sigma and ‖g‖2≥4​σ2/c\|g\|_{2}\geq 4\sigma^{2}/c, the proof takes λ⁡(g)=⟨μ⁡(g),g⟩/‖g‖22\lambda(g)=\langle\mu(g),g\rangle/\|g\|_{2}^{2}, so the residual is the component orthogonal to gg of 𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)​ξ]=𝔼⁡[(ac​(g+ξ)−ac​(g))​ξ]\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)\xi]=\mathbb{E}[(a_{c}(g+\xi)-a_{c}(g))\xi], which is second order in ξ\xi by the two-point estimate |ac​(y)−ac​(g)|≤ac​(y)​ac​(g)​‖y−g‖2/c|a_{c}(y)-a_{c}(g)|\leq a_{c}(y)a_{c}(g)\|y-g\|_{2}/c. When c≥σc\geq\sigma and ‖g‖2<4​σ2/c\|g\|_{2}<4\sigma^{2}/c, it takes λ​(g)=ac​(g)\lambda(g)=a_{c}(g), and the residual contains in addition the longitudinal term (𝔼​ac​(g+ξ)−ac​(g))​g(\mathbb{E}\,a_{c}(g+\xi)-a_{c}(g))g, which the same estimate bounds by 4​ac​(g)​σ2/c4a_{c}(g)\sigma^{2}/c because gg is small. When c<σc<\sigma and ‖g‖2≫σ\|g\|_{2}\gg\sigma, most per-example gradients are clipped onto a cone around gg. Both cases use only the centered variance (proofs in Appendix B.2). Koloskova et al. (2023) bound the additive deviation ‖μ⁡(g)−clipc​(g)‖2\|\mu(g)-\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g)\|_{2} from the same ray, since clipc​(g)=ac​(g)​g\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g)=a_{c}(g)g; the new element here is that the deviation is bounded relative to λ⁡(g)\lambda(g), uniformly in ‖g‖2\|g\|_{2}, which is exactly what a scale-invariant update needs. Relatedly, Xiao et al. (2023) identify the sampling noise of the gradients being clipped as a key source of the bias of clipped and normalized DP-SGD.

The second ingredient translates a small projective error into a descent direction.

Lemma 2 (Projective LMO bound).

For all m,g∈𝒳⋆m,g\in\mathcal{X}^{\star} and d∈LMO⁡(m)d\in\mathrm{LMO}(m),

⟨g,d⟩≤−‖g‖⋆+2​ℛ​(m,g),\langle g,d\rangle\ \leq\ -\|g\|_{\star}+2\,\mathcal{R}(m,g),

where ℛ⁡(m,g):=infλ>0‖m−λ​g‖⋆/λ\mathcal{R}(m,g):=\inf_{\lambda>0}\|m-\lambda g\|_{\star}/\lambda.

This is the normalized-step inequality of Cutkosky and Mehta (2020, Lemma 2) (see also Pethick et al., 2025) applied to m/λm/\lambda, using LMO⁡(m)=LMO⁡(m/λ)\mathrm{LMO}(m)=\mathrm{LMO}(m/\lambda) and optimizing over λ\lambda. Unlike the additive bias ‖m−g‖⋆\|m-g\|_{\star}, ℛ⁡(m,g)\mathcal{R}(m,g) vanishes whenever mm is any positive multiple of gg.

The first condition in (3) ties the stepsize to the clipping threshold and the momentum: the iterates must move slowly enough that the clipping scales λ​(∇f​(xk))\lambda(\nabla f(x_{k})) seen by the momentum buffer change by at most a constant factor over its effective window 1/α1/\alpha. The second requires the filtered privacy noise to be smaller than the clipping radius, which is the norm of the clipped signal when gradients are large. Because the noise is controlled through its worst-case dual norm 𝔼​‖Z‖⋆\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star}, this condition is restrictive: in the experiments of Section 4, even in the optimistic ℓ2\ell_{2} specialization it holds, together with the run-in requirement T>0T>0, only for CIFAR-10 at the largest batch size with momentum 0.990.99, for no language-modeling configuration, and not at the observed optima; in the spectral geometry of DP-Muon, where H2/dH^{2}/d grows with the matrix rank, it holds for none of our configurations (Appendix D.2 gives the numbers).

The fixed-noise rate matches the K−1/4K^{-1/4} rate of normalized SGD with momentum (Cutkosky and Mehta, 2020) and of clipped SGD (Koloskova et al., 2023) (the first-moment counterpart of the K−1/2K^{-1/2} squared-norm rate: a squared-norm rate implies ours by Jensen’s inequality, not conversely), which is optimal under bounded variance (Arjevani et al., 2023), up to the (log⁡K)1/4(\log K)^{1/4} factor from the high-probability bound over the privacy noise. For the ℓ2\ell_{2} geometry, H≈dH\approx\sqrt{d} and the calibrated bound is the usual nonconvex DP-SGD dependence (d​log⁡(1/δ))1/4/n​ε(d\log(1/\delta))^{1/4}/\sqrt{n\varepsilon}. The privacy term of the bound is below the initial gradient bound 2​L​Φ0\sqrt{2L\Phi_{0}} when n​ε≳c​H​log⁡(1/δ)/L​Φ0n\varepsilon\gtrsim cH\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/\sqrt{L\Phi_{0}}, but the whole bound is nontrivial only if, in addition, the clipping floor b~c\widetilde{b}_{c}, which does not depend on n​εn\varepsilon, is small compared with L​Φ0\sqrt{L\Phi_{0}}. The condition on n​εn\varepsilon in Corollary 1 is stronger than this threshold by the factor ρ22​L​Φ0/c2\rho_{2}^{2}L\Phi_{0}/c^{2} whenever c≲L​Φ0c\lesssim\sqrt{L\Phi_{0}}, that is, the requirement on n​εn\varepsilon grows with the ratio of the gradient scale to the clipping threshold, which is the price of not assuming bounded gradients (Appendix C.2). For the spectral geometry, 𝔼​‖Z‖⋆\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star} is the nuclear norm of a Gaussian matrix, of order min⁡{m,n′}​max⁡{m,n′}\min\{m,n^{\prime}\}\sqrt{\max\{m,n^{\prime}\}} (Table 2), and the bound controls the nuclear norm of the gradient. Translated to Frobenius stationarity, the ratio of the leading privacy terms of the spectral and Euclidean bounds is (Lop/LF)1/4​r1/4/s0(L_{\rm op}/L_{F})^{1/4}\,r^{1/4}/s_{0}, where r=min⁡{m,n′}r=\min\{m,n^{\prime}\}, LopL_{\rm op} and LFL_{F} are the smoothness constants of Assumption 1 in the two geometries, and s0∈[1,r]s_{0}\in[1,\sqrt{r}] is such that ‖∇f‖nuc≥s0​‖∇f‖F\|\nabla f\|_{\rm nuc}\geq s_{0}\|\nabla f\|_{F} along the trajectory. For gradients with a flat spectrum (s0=rs_{0}=\sqrt{r}) and comparable smoothness constants this is a gain of r−1/4r^{-1/4}, for rank-one gradients a loss of r1/4r^{1/4}, and the gain disappears when Lop/LFL_{\rm op}/L_{F} grows like rr, as it does for f=12​‖X‖F2f=\tfrac{1}{2}\|X\|_{F}^{2}; the advantage of the spectral geometry therefore rests on Lop≪r​LFL_{\rm op}\ll rL_{F}, which is the premise of Muon itself. This compares only the leading privacy terms: after the same conversion, the clipping floor b~c=ρ1​min⁡{σ,σ2/c}\widetilde{b}_{c}=\rho_{1}\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\}, with ρ1=r\rho_{1}=\sqrt{r} in the spectral geometry, is r/s0\sqrt{r}/s_{0} times its Euclidean counterpart, so the two floors coincide for flat spectra and the spectral one is larger by r\sqrt{r} for rank-one gradients. The worst-case dual-norm treatment of the noise is the price of the generality in the norm.

Proof sketch.

The LMO is invariant to the bias-correction factor of the momentum, so we work with m¯k=∑t≤kwk,t​g^t\overline{m}_{k}=\sum_{t\leq k}w_{k,t}\hat{g}_{t}, ∑twk,t=1\sum_{t}w_{k,t}=1. By Lemma 1, m¯k=Ak∇f(xk)+Dk+∑twk,trt+Nk+Pk\overline{m}_{k}=A_{k}\nabla f(x_{k})+D_{k}+\sum_{t}w_{k,t}r_{t}+N_{k}+P_{k} with Ak=∑twk,t​λtA_{k}=\sum_{t}w_{k,t}\lambda_{t}, a drift term DkD_{k}, sampling noise NkN_{k}, and privacy noise PkP_{k}. Lemma 2 with λ=Ak\lambda=A_{k} reduces the descent step to bounding each term divided by AkA_{k}. The residuals contribute 16​b~c16\widetilde{b}_{c}. The first condition in (3) keeps AkA_{k} within a constant factor of ac​(∇f​(xk))a_{c}(\nabla f(x_{k})), which controls the drift (≲L​γ/α\lesssim L\gamma/\alpha) and, with the variance bound of Lemma 1, the sampling noise. Gaussian concentration bounds ‖Pk‖⋆≤νDP​(η)\|P_{k}\|_{\star}\leq\nu_{\rm DP}(\eta) for all kk, and dividing by AkA_{k} produces the ‖∇f​(xk)‖⋆\|\nabla f(x_{k})\|_{\star}-proportional term absorbed by the second condition. Full proofs are in Appendix B.

3.3 Comparison with existing guarantees

Table 1 compares guarantees for mechanisms that clip individual examples before aggregation, as DP-SGD and Algorithm 1 do. Two points deserve emphasis. First, our clipping floor ρ1​min⁡{σ,σ2/c}\rho_{1}\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\} is the dual-norm version of the floor of Koloskova et al. (2023), which is tight for clipped SGD under bounded variance; passing through a non-Euclidean LMO thus costs only the norm-conversion constant ρ1\rho_{1}. Second, the floor depends only on the centered variance and vanishes as σ→0\sigma\to 0, even when ‖∇f‖2≫c\|\nabla f\|_{2}\gg c. In contrast, the general bound of Kim and Fan (2026) contains a clipping term of the form 𝔼​(‖∇fi‖−c)+\mathbb{E}(\|\nabla f_{i}\|-c)_{+}, which persists for deterministic gradients larger than cc, and their vanishing-rate corollaries require moment bounds on raw gradients, which by 1n​∑i‖∇fi‖22=‖∇f‖22+1n​∑i‖∇fi−∇f‖22\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\|\nabla f_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\nabla f\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\|\nabla f_{i}-\nabla f\|_{2}^{2} also bound the mean gradient, together with a threshold growing with KK. Outside privacy, Cutkosky and Mehta (2021) analyze the same clip–momentum–normalize pipeline in general norms under heavy-tailed noise, with an additive clipping bias controlled by a threshold that grows with the horizon. Rates are stated under different conventions (fixed noise versus calibrated noise, average versus minimum, norm versus squared norm), which we align in Appendix E.

4 Experiments

Setup.

We compare DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon (along with DP-Scion for language modeling) against their non-private counterparts on CIFAR-10 image classification (Krizhevsky, 2009) and on language modeling using a 30M-parameter NanoGPT model. To approximate the orthogonalization update, we utilize the Newton-Schulz method Jordan et al. (2024) with 5 iterations. DP training uses Opacus (Yousefpour et al., 2021) with Poisson subsampling (our analysis uses fixed-size batches), clipping threshold c=1c=1 following De et al. (2022), ε=8\varepsilon=8, and δ=1/(2​n)\delta=1/(2n). For each optimizer and batch size BB we grid-search the learning rate and the momentum 1−α1-\alpha, with zero weight decay; grids are listed in Appendix G. To make models compatible with per-example clipping, BatchNorm layers are replaced by GroupNorm and biases are disabled in all linear layers. We report the best value over the grid for each BB. The CIFAR-10 curves average three seeds; all language-modeling results and all heatmaps are single runs. For DP-SGD on CIFAR-10 (B≥256B\geq 256) and for Scion at B=16,384B=16{,}384, the best learning rate lies at the upper end of the grid (Appendix G), so these baselines may be slightly under-tuned. Note that the hyperparameter search itself is not included in the privacy accounting, as is common in the DP literature (Papernot and Steinke, 2022). Note that we utilize standard momentum for SGD and Muon optimizers (equivalent to nesterov=False in PyTorch).

Image classification.

We train the CIFAR Airbench architecture (Jordan, 2024) (2M parameters). Without privacy (Figure 1, left), Muon attains the lowest test loss at every batch size, with its minimum (below 1.051.05) at B=256B=256, whereas Adam and SGD are best at B≤128B\leq 128. With privacy (right), the picture changes in two ways. First, all optimizers prefer batches that are one to two orders of magnitude larger, with minima at B=5000B=5000–1000010000, in line with prior observations for DP-SGD (De et al., 2022; Sander et al., 2023). Second, the gaps between optimizers largely disappear: for 128≤B≤1024128\leq B\leq 1024 the three curves overlap within one standard deviation. DP-Muon attains the lowest mean loss at every batch size except B=10000B=10000, where DP-SGD is marginally better, but the differences exceed one standard deviation only at the extremes B=64B=64 and B=25000B=25000, where DP-Muon degrades the least. Across privacy levels at B=1024B=1024 (Appendix G.2), DP-Muon is on par with or slightly better than DP-SGD and DP-Adam for ε∈{1,5,8}\varepsilon\in\{1,5,8\}, with the largest margin over DP-Adam at ε=1\varepsilon=1; at ε=3\varepsilon=3 the three methods are within noise.

Language modeling.

The model consists of 6 layers, 6 attention heads, an embedding dimension of 384, and a vocabulary of 50,304 tokens. It is trained on sequences of length 1,024 for 600 million tokens from the 10-billion-token subset of FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024), equating to roughly 20 tokens per parameter.

The training set is a fixed random subset of n≈5.86⋅105n\approx 5.86\cdot 10^{5} sequences from this pool, processed for one epoch with Poisson sampling rate q=B/nq=B/n and δ=1/(2​n)\delta=1/(2n); this translates to approximately 18,300 steps for a batch size of B=32B=32, down to 36 steps for a maximum batch size of B=16,384B=16{,}384. We define a single sequence of 1,024 tokens as the privacy unit, so a document that spans several sequences is not protected as a whole.

In the non-private baseline, the performance ranking (Muon << Adam << SGD) holds across all batch sizes, and Muon’s advantage grows with BB (achieving a final loss of 4.10 versus 4.82 for Adam at B=1024B=1024). Under differential privacy (right), the optimal batch size shifts from 32–64 up to 1024–4096, and the optimizer ranking becomes dependent on BB. DP-Muon has the lowest loss for B≤256B\leq 256, by at most 0.090.09 nats in single runs; DP-Adam is optimal for 512≤B≤2048512\leq B\leq 2048 and attains the lowest overall loss (6.33 at B=1024B=1024, versus 6.51 for DP-Muon at B=2048B=2048); and DP-Scion, which utilizes sign updates for the embedding and output layers, performs best for B≥4096B\geq 4096 and exhibits the least degradation at very large batch sizes. At their respective optimal batch sizes, the four optimizers are within 0.25 nats of each other, compared to a gap of 0.9 nats between Muon and SGD without privacy.

What changes under privacy.

We highlight three findings. (i) Batch size is the dominant hyperparameter on both tasks: at a fixed budget of epochs or tokens, the optimal batch size grows by a factor of 15–300, and the ranking of optimizers depends on it, so conclusions drawn at a single batch size, or transferred from non-private training, can be misleading. In both tasks the root-mean-square size of the privacy noise exceeds the root-mean-square bound c/Bc/\sqrt{B} on the sampling noise of clipped gradients by one to two orders of magnitude at every batch size and decays with BB faster than B−1/2B^{-1/2}, and the observed optima lie where its norm becomes comparable to the clipping radius (Figure 3, Appendix D.1). There, the noise-to-signal ratio is about 44–2727 times larger than the admissibility condition of Theorem 1 allows for 1−α=0.91-\alpha=0.9, so the theorem does not cover these configurations and does not explain the location of the optima (Appendix D.2). The dependence of the ranking on the batch size is consistent with reports of large gains for private Muon at large batches in vision (Shanmugam et al., 2026). (ii) The learning rate of DP-Muon grows with the batch size: for language modeling, from 0.050.05 at B≤512B\leq 512 to 0.20.2 at B≥8192B\geq 8192, whereas the optimal learning rate of DP-Adam stays within [10−3,3⋅10−3][10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-3}] and, without privacy, the optimal learning rate of every method on language modeling is the same at all batch sizes (Appendix G.3). (iii) DP-Muon is insensitive to the momentum: for DP language modeling, at the optimal learning rate, its loss varies by about 0.10.1 nats or less over momentum values 1−α∈[0.8,0.95]1-\alpha\in[0.8,0.95] at every batch size, so the selected momentum appears erratic across batch sizes (Appendix G.3). This is compatible with Theorem 1, in which a longer momentum window 1/α1/\alpha reduces the filtered sampling and privacy noise (∝α\propto\sqrt{\alpha}) but increases the tracking error (∝L​γ/α\propto L\gamma/\alpha).

5 Related Work

LMO-based methods.

Beyond Scion and the trust-region analyses of Kovalev (2025); Kovalev and Borodich (2025), LMO-based methods include the layer-wise Gluon (Riabinin et al., 2025), and the effect of replacing the polar factor by a few Newton–Schulz steps is analyzed by Shulgin et al. (2025) and Kim and Oh (2026). None of these works consider per-example clipping or privacy noise; distributed and compressed variants are discussed in Appendix F.

Clipping in private optimization.

Analyses of per-example clipping are compared in Section 3.3. A complementary line replaces clipping by per-sample normalization, which removes the threshold (Bu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022); we instead keep the standard clipping of DP-SGD and normalize only the aggregated momentum through the LMO. Nonlinear post-processing of privatized gradients creates its own bias, which can be corrected for Adam (Tang et al., 2024) and for Newton–Schulz (Kim and Fan, 2026).

Training dynamics and hyperparameters under privacy.

Large batches are crucial for accurate private training (De et al., 2022); Sander et al. (2023) show that the performance of DP-SGD is governed mainly by the total amount of injected noise, which allows hyperparameters to be tuned at small batch sizes, Panda et al. (2024) propose a linear scaling rule to transfer hyperparameters across privacy budgets, McKenna et al. (2025) derive scaling laws for private language models, and Papernot and Steinke (2022) account for the privacy cost of tuning. Under privacy, the noise dominates Adam’s second-moment estimate, so that DP-Adam behaves like DP-SGD unless corrected (Tang et al., 2024), and Monzio Compagnoni et al. (2026) compare DP-SignSGD with DP-SGD through stochastic differential equations. For non-private LMO methods, Shulgin et al. (2026) derive hyperparameter scaling laws by minimizing convergence bounds of the same form as Theorem 1.

6 Conclusion and Limitations

Muon is compatible with differential privacy because, for a scale-invariant update, the leading effect of per-example clipping is a harmless rescaling; the remaining directional bias is controlled by the centered variance alone, which yields convergence guarantees for private momentum-LMO methods in any norm whose clipping floor matches that of clipped SGD up to the norm-conversion constant ρ1\rho_{1}. Empirically, privacy makes the batch size the dominant hyperparameter and reorders optimizers, so DP-Muon is most beneficial in some batch-size regimes rather than uniformly. Our analysis has limitations: it assumes an exact LMO rather than a few Newton–Schulz steps and fixed-size batches, whereas our experiments use Poisson subsampling; it treats the Gaussian noise through worst-case dual-norm bounds, which leads to the admissibility condition in (3) and excludes the hyperparameter regime of our experiments (entirely in the spectral geometry of DP-Muon, and except for CIFAR-10 at the largest batch size in the ℓ2\ell_{2} specialization); and its fixed-threshold bound retains a clipping floor. Our language-modeling experiments are small-scale pretraining from scratch; private fine-tuning of pretrained models (Li et al., 2022a; Kim and Fan, 2026) is a natural next step.

Appendix A Prerequisites

Throughout the appendix, Assumptions 1 and 2 from Section 2 hold.

Definition 2 (Dual norm).

Let (𝒳,∥⋅∥)(\mathcal{X},\|\cdot\|) be a finite-dimensional normed vector space with dual space 𝒳⋆\mathcal{X}^{\star}. The dual norm is

‖v‖⋆:=sup‖d‖≤1⟨v,d⟩,v∈𝒳⋆.\|v\|_{\star}:=\sup_{\|d\|\leq 1}\langle v,d\rangle,\quad v\in\mathcal{X}^{\star}.
Definition 3 (Linear minimization oracle (LMO)).

For 𝒞={x∈𝒳:‖x‖≤1}\mathcal{C}=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:\|x\|\leq 1\}, LMO⁡(v):=arg⁡mind∈𝒞​⟨v,d⟩\operatorname{LMO}(v):=\arg\min_{d\in\mathcal{C}}\langle v,d\rangle for v∈𝒳⋆v\in\mathcal{X}^{\star}; when the minimizer is not unique, any minimizer may be used.

Corollary 2.

For any d∈LMO⁡(v)d\in\operatorname{LMO}(v), Definitions 2 and 3 give ⟨v,d⟩=−‖v‖⋆\langle v,d\rangle=-\|v\|_{\star}; moreover, LMO⁡(λ​v)=LMO⁡(v)\operatorname{LMO}(\lambda v)=\operatorname{LMO}(v) for every λ>0\lambda>0.

Definition 4 (Norm-equivalence constants).

Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite-dimensional, there exist ρ1,ρ2>0\rho_{1},\rho_{2}>0 such that

‖v‖⋆≤ρ1​‖v‖2,‖v‖2≤ρ2​‖v‖⋆∀v∈𝒳⋆.\|v\|_{\star}\leq\rho_{1}\|v\|_{2},\qquad\|v\|_{2}\leq\rho_{2}\|v\|_{\star}\qquad\forall v\in\mathcal{X}^{\star}. (4)

Table 2 lists the LMO, the constants ρ1,ρ2\rho_{1},\rho_{2}, and the order of 𝔼​‖Z‖⋆\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star} for Z∼𝒩⁡(0,I)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) (which enters the privacy-noise term) for common geometries.

By Assumption 1, for all x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X},

f⁡(y)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+L2​‖y−x‖2.f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^{2}. (5)
Corollary 3.

For every xx, write ∇fi​(x)=∇f​(x)+ξi\nabla f_{i}(x)=\nabla f(x)+\xi_{i} with i∼Unif⁡[n]i\sim\mathrm{Unif}[n]. By Assumption 2,

𝔼i​[ξi]=1n​∑i=1nξi=0,𝔼i​[‖ξi‖22]=1n​∑i=1n‖ξi‖22≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{i}[\xi_{i}]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{i}[\|\xi_{i}\|^{2}_{2}]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\xi_{i}\|^{2}_{2}\leq\sigma^{2}.

Define the clipping factor

ac​(v):=cmax⁡{c,‖v‖2},so thatclipc​(v)=ac​(v)​v.a_{c}(v):=\frac{c}{\max\{c,\|v\|_{2}\}},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad\mathrm{clip}_{c}(v)=a_{c}(v)\,v.
Corollary 4.

Since v↦max⁡{c,‖v‖2}v\mapsto\max\{c,\|v\|_{2}\} is 11-Lipschitz,

|ac​(y)−ac​(x)|≤ac​(y)​ac​(x)c​‖y−x‖2.|a_{c}(y)-a_{c}(x)|\leq\frac{a_{c}(y)a_{c}(x)}{c}\|y-x\|_{2}. (6)

Appendix B DP-Muon convergence

B.1 Notation

Let:

f⁡(x):=1n​∑i=1nfi​(x),n=|𝒟|.f(x):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(x),\quad n=|\mathcal{D}|.

At iteration k, independently of previous sampling and Gaussian noise, draw

Sk∼Unif​{S⊆[n]:|S|=B}.S_{k}\sim\text{Unif}\{S\subseteq[n]:|S|=B\}.

And compute private averaged gradient

g^k=1B​∑i∈Skclipc​(∇fi​(xk))+zk.\hat{g}_{k}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in S_{k}}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(\nabla f_{i}(x_{k}))+z_{k}.

We define the clipped mini-batch average:

g¯k=1B​∑i∈Skclipc​(∇fi​(xk)).\bar{g}_{k}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in S_{k}}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(\nabla f_{i}(x_{k})).

In the subsequent lemmas, we will use a simplified notation. Assuming a deterministic vector gg and a stochastic noise vector ξi\xi_{i} satisfying Corollary 3, we write:

μ⁡(g):=1n​∑i=1nclipc​(g+ξi).\mu(g):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi_{i}).

We inject Gaussian privacy noise:

zk∼𝒩⁡(0,c2​σDP2​I),𝔼⁡[zk]=0,𝔼​‖zk‖22=:d​c2​σDP2.z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,c^{2}\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{DP}}I),\qquad\mathbb{E}[z_{k}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\|z_{k}\|_{2}^{2}=:dc^{2}\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{DP}}.

From the algorithm definition, the overall oracle is:

g^k:=g¯k+zk.\hat{g}_{k}:=\bar{g}_{k}+z_{k}. (7)

For notational convenience, define

σ~:=ρ1​σ,b~c:=ρ1​min⁡{σ,σ2c}.\widetilde{\sigma}:=\rho_{1}\sigma,\qquad\widetilde{b}_{c}:=\rho_{1}\min\left\{\sigma,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c}\right\}. (8)

Define the pre-batch filtration representing the complete history of the algorithm prior to drawing the batch StS_{t} and privacy noise ztz_{t} (xtx_{t} is determined):

ℱt:=σ⁡(x0,{Ss,zs}s=0t−1).\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma(x_{0},\{S_{s},z_{s}\}_{s=0}^{t-1}). (9)

B.2 Useful lemmas

Lemma 1 in the main text combines Lemmas 4 and 5 below, and Lemma 2 is Lemma 3.

Throughout this subsection ξ\xi denotes ξi\xi_{i} with i∼Unif​[n]i\sim\text{Unif}[n], and 𝔼\mathbb{E}, ℙ\mathbb{P} are with respect to i; by Corollary 3, 𝔼​ξ=0\mathbb{E}\xi=0 and 𝔼​‖ξ‖22≤σ2\mathbb{E}\|\xi\|_{2}^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}.

For m,g∈𝒳⋆m,g\in\mathcal{X}^{\star}, define the error

ℛ⁡(m,g):=infλ>0‖m−λ​g‖⋆λ.\mathcal{R}(m,g):=\inf_{\lambda>0}\frac{\|m-\lambda g\|_{\star}}{\lambda}. (10)
Lemma 3 (Inner Product Bound).

Let d∈LMO⁡(m)d\in\operatorname{LMO}(m). Then

⟨g,d⟩≤−‖g‖⋆+2​ℛ​(m,g).\langle g,d\rangle\leq-\|g\|_{\star}+2\mathcal{R}(m,g). (11)
Proof.

Fix any λ>0\lambda>0. By Corollary 2,

λ​⟨g,d⟩\displaystyle\lambda\langle g,d\rangle =⟨m,d⟩−⟨m−λ​g,d⟩\displaystyle=\langle m,d\rangle-\langle m-\lambda g,d\rangle
≤−‖m‖⋆+‖m−λ​g‖⋆\displaystyle\leq-\|m\|_{\star}+\|m-\lambda g\|_{\star}
≤−λ​‖g‖⋆+2​‖m−λ​g‖⋆.\displaystyle\leq-\lambda\|g\|_{\star}+2\|m-\lambda g\|_{\star}.

Divide by λ\lambda and take the infimum over λ>0\lambda>0. ∎

Lemma 4 (Clipping Bias Smooth Bound).

For every gg, there exists a scalar λ⁡(g)>0\lambda(g)>0 such that

14​ac​(g)≤λ⁡(g)≤2​ac​(g),\frac{1}{4}a_{c}(g)\leq\lambda(g)\leq 2a_{c}(g), (12)

and

‖μ⁡(g)−λ⁡(g)​g‖2≤16​λ​(g)​min⁡{σ,σ2c}.\|\mu(g)-\lambda(g)g\|_{2}\leq 16\lambda(g)\min\left\{\sigma,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c}\right\}.

Consequently,

‖μ⁡(g)−λ⁡(g)​g‖⋆≤16​λ​(g)​b~c.\|\mu(g)-\lambda(g)g\|_{\star}\leq 16\lambda(g)\widetilde{b}_{c}.
Proof.

Case 1: c≥σc\geq\sigma. Since

max⁡{c,‖g+ξ‖2}≤max⁡{c,‖g‖2}+‖ξ‖2,\max\{c,\|g+\xi\|_{2}\}\leq\max\{c,\|g\|_{2}\}+\|\xi\|_{2},

we have

ac​(g+ξ)=cmax⁡{c,‖g+ξ‖2}≥cmax⁡{c,‖g‖2}+‖ξ‖2=ac​(g)1+ac​(g)​‖ξ‖2/c.a_{c}(g+\xi)=\frac{c}{\max\{c,\|g+\xi\|_{2}\}}\geq\frac{c}{\max\{c,\|g\|_{2}\}+\|\xi\|_{2}}=\frac{a_{c}(g)}{1+a_{c}(g)\|\xi\|_{2}/c}.

The map t↦(1+t)−1t\mapsto(1+t)^{-1} is convex on [0,∞)[0,\infty), hence by Jensen’s inequality:

𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)]≥ac​(g)1+ac​(g)​𝔼​‖ξ‖2/c≥ac​(g)2,\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)]\geq\frac{a_{c}(g)}{1+a_{c}(g)\mathbb{E}\|\xi\|_{2}/c}\geq\frac{a_{c}(g)}{2},

where we used 𝔼​‖ξ‖2≤σ≤c\mathbb{E}\|\xi\|_{2}\leq\sigma\leq c.

Using 𝔼⁡[ξ]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi]=0 and (6):

‖𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)​ξ]‖2=‖𝔼⁡[(ac​(g+ξ)−ac​(g))​ξ]‖2≤ac​(g)c​𝔼​[ac​(g+ξ)​‖ξ‖22]≤ac​(g)​σ2c.\left\|\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)\xi]\right\|_{2}=\left\|\mathbb{E}[(a_{c}(g+\xi)-a_{c}(g))\xi]\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{a_{c}(g)}{c}\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)\|\xi\|_{2}^{2}]\leq a_{c}(g)\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c}. (13)

Suppose first that

‖g‖2≥4​σ2c.\|g\|_{2}\geq\frac{4\sigma^{2}}{c}.

Define

λ⁡(g):=⟨μ⁡(g),g/‖g‖2⟩‖g‖2=⟨μ⁡(g),g⟩‖g‖22.\lambda(g):=\frac{\langle\mu(g),g/\|g\|_{2}\rangle}{\|g\|_{2}}=\frac{\langle\mu(g),g\rangle}{\|g\|^{2}_{2}}.

Since

μ⁡(g)=𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)​(g+ξ)]=𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)]​g+𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)​ξ],\mu(g)=\mathbb{E}\big[a_{c}(g+\xi)(g+\xi)\big]=\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)]g+\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)\xi],

previously proven bound 𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)]≥ac​(g)2\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)]\geq\frac{a_{c}(g)}{2}, ‖𝔼⁡[ac​(g+ξ)​ξ]‖2≤ac​(g)​σ2c\left\|\mathbb{E}[a_{c}(g+\xi)\xi]\right\|_{2}\leq a_{c}(g)\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c} and Cauchy–Schwarz imply:

Lemma 5 (Clipping Variance).

With the notation of Lemma 4,

𝔼⁡[‖clipc​(g+ξ)−μ⁡(g)‖22]≤20​ac​(g)2​σ2≤320​λ​(g)2​σ2.\mathbb{E}\left[\|\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi)-\mu(g)\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq 20a_{c}(g)^{2}\sigma^{2}\leq 320\lambda(g)^{2}\sigma^{2}. (14)

Outside the ball, the clipping operator is the radial projection clip⁡(v)=c​v/‖v‖2\mathrm{clip}(v)=cv/\|v\|_{2}. Its Jacobian matrix is:

Jclip​(v)=c‖v‖2​(I−v​v⊤‖v‖22).J_{\mathrm{clip}}(v)=\frac{c}{\|v\|_{2}}\left(I-\frac{vv^{\top}}{\|v\|_{2}^{2}}\right).

‖clipc​(g+ξ)−clipc​(g)‖2≤(maxv⁡‖Jclip​(v)‖2)​‖(g+ξ)−g‖2≤2​ac​(g)​‖ξ‖2.\|\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g+\xi)-\mathrm{clip}_{c}(g)\|_{2}\leq\left(\max_{v}\|J_{\mathrm{clip}}(v)\|_{2}\right)\|(g+\xi)-g\|_{2}\leq 2a_{c}(g)\|\xi\|_{2}.

≤4​ac​(g)2​σ2+4​ac​(g)2​‖g‖22​(4​σ2‖g‖22)\displaystyle\leq 4a_{c}(g)^{2}\sigma^{2}+4a_{c}(g)^{2}\|g\|_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{4\sigma^{2}}{\|g\|_{2}^{2}}\right)

Under Assumptions 1–2, the iterates of Algorithm 1 satisfy, for every γ>0\gamma>0, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), and K≥1K\geq 1,

1K​∑k=0K−1𝔼​‖gk‖⋆≤Φ0K​γ+L​γ2+32​b~c+2K​∑k=0K−1𝔼⁡[‖Dk‖⋆Ak+‖Nk‖⋆Ak+‖Pk‖⋆Ak],\boxed{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\|g_{k}\|_{\star}\leq\frac{\Phi_{0}}{K\gamma}+\frac{L\gamma}{2}+32\widetilde{b}_{c}+\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{\|D_{k}\|_{\star}}{A_{k}}+\frac{\|N_{k}\|_{\star}}{A_{k}}+\frac{\|P_{k}\|_{\star}}{A_{k}}\big],} (18)

B.6 Privacy-noise bound

Let Z∼𝒩⁡(0,I)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). The map z↦‖z‖⋆z\mapsto\|z\|_{\star} is ρ1\rho_{1}-Lipschitz with respect to ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2}. To evaluate this variance multiplier, we explicitly sum the squares of the normalized exponential moving average weights wk,t=α​(1−α)k−t1−(1−α)k+1w_{k,t}=\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)^{k-t}}{1-(1-\alpha)^{k+1}}:

=α2(1−(1−α)k+1)2​1−(1−α)2​(k+1)1−(1−α)2\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{(1-(1-\alpha)^{k+1})^{2}}\frac{1-(1-\alpha)^{2(k+1)}}{1-(1-\alpha)^{2}}
=α2(1−(1−α)k+1)2​(1−(1−α)k+1)​(1+(1−α)k+1)α⁡(2−α)\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{(1-(1-\alpha)^{k+1})^{2}}\frac{(1-(1-\alpha)^{k+1})(1+(1-\alpha)^{k+1})}{\alpha(2-\alpha)}
=α2−α​1+(1−α)k+11−(1−α)k+1.\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha}{2-\alpha}\frac{1+(1-\alpha)^{k+1}}{1-(1-\alpha)^{k+1}}.

For k≥kb=⌈log⁡2α⌉k\geq k_{\rm b}=\lceil\frac{\log 2}{\alpha}\rceil, we have (1−α)k+1≤12(1-\alpha)^{k+1}\leq\frac{1}{2}, so the right-hand side is at most 3​α3\alpha. Therefore Pk​=𝑑​sk​ZP_{k}\overset{d}{=}s_{k}Z with Z∼𝒩⁡(0,I)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and sk≤3​α​c​σDPs_{k}\leq\sqrt{3\alpha}\,c\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}, and ‖Pk‖⋆\|P_{k}\|_{\star} is stochastically dominated by 3​α​c​σDP​‖Z‖⋆\sqrt{3\alpha}\,c\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}\|Z\|_{\star}.

To bound the dual norm of this noise, we apply the Tsirelson-Ibragimov-Sudakov concentration inequality. For the standard Gaussian vector ZZ and the ρ1\rho_{1}-Lipschitz mapping z↦‖z‖⋆z\mapsto\|z\|_{\star}, the one-sided tail bound is:

ℙ⁡(‖Z‖⋆−𝔼​‖Z‖⋆≥t)≤exp⁡(−t22​ρ12).\mathbb{P}\Big(\|Z\|_{\star}-\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star}\geq t\Big)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\rho_{1}^{2}}\right).

To guarantee a global failure probability of at most η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) across the TT tail iterations, we allocate a failure budget of η/T\eta/T to each step. Setting the right-hand side to η/T\eta/T yields the deviation threshold t=ρ1​2​log⁡(T/η)t=\rho_{1}\sqrt{2\log(T/\eta)}. HT,η:=𝔼​‖Z‖⋆+ρ1​2​log⁡(Tη),Z∼𝒩⁡(0,I),H_{T,\eta}:=\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star}+\rho_{1}\sqrt{2\log\left(\frac{T}{\eta}\right)},\quad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),
νDP​(η):=c​σDP​3​α​HT,η,\nu_{\rm DP}(\eta):=c\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}\sqrt{3\alpha}\,H_{T,\eta}, (26)
